JSON: Name: mtorc1_ilc2_nmur1_epigenetic_axis Title: Genetic and pharmacological perturbation and epigenetic profiling of mTORC1-regulated NMUR1 in lung ILC2s to modulate neuro-immune crosstalk in allergic asthma Short Hypothesis: Activation of mTORC1 in lung ILC2s increases NMUR1 expression via acetyl-CoA–dependent histone acetylation at the Nmur1 promoter, thereby enhancing NMU-driven IL-5 and IL-13 production and exacerbating allergic airway inflammation. Related Work: Prior work has established that ILC2s drive type 2 airway inflammation in response to epithelial alarmins (IL-33, IL-25) and neuronal peptides (NMU), and that mTORC1 is a central regulator of cellular metabolism and immune cell effector programs. Studies have shown mTORC1 involvement in T cell and ILC metabolic control and that NMUR1–NMU signaling amplifies ILC2 cytokine output. Existing approaches have used single-axis interventions (e.g., cytokine blockade, NMU pathway perturbation, or systemic rapamycin) but do not resolve how metabolic state controls expression of sensory receptors on ILC2s or define the epigenetic intermediates linking metabolism to receptor transcription. Limitations include incomplete cell-intrinsic versus systemic attribution of pharmacologic effects, limited mechanistic connection between nutrient/metabolite flux and specific receptor loci, tissue-specific differences in mTORC1 requirements across ILC2 niches, and sparse translational data linking human ILC2 metabolic-epigenetic states to receptor expression. Abstract: Allergic asthma initiation involves lung-resident group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) that integrate epithelial and neuronal signals; however, the mechanisms by which cellular metabolism controls expression of neuronal-sensing receptors on ILC2s remain unresolved. We propose to test whether mTORC1 activity in lung ILC2s drives NMUR1 expression through metabolite-dependent histone acetylation and thereby potentiates NMU-stimulated type 2 cytokine production and airway inflammation. Using combined genetic (Raptor deletion in ILC2s) and pharmacological (rapamycin, ATP-citrate lyase and HAT inhibitors) perturbations, integrated with metabolic flux assays, chromatin immunoprecipitation and epigenomic profiling, and functional allergen and NMU challenge models, we will determine the causal chain from mTORC1 → acetyl-CoA → H3 acetylation at Nmur1 → NMUR1 protein → ILC2 effector function. Main contributions will be (1) demonstration of an mTORC1-dependent metabolic–epigenetic mechanism controlling receptor expression on tissue-resident lymphocytes, (2) direct evidence of NMUR1 as a modifiable amplifier of neuro-immune crosstalk in allergic lung inflammation, and (3) evaluation of receptor- vs metabolism-targeted interventions as modulators of ILC2-driven pathology. Expected outcomes include identification of mechanistic biomarkers and proof-of-concept targets to reduce ILC2-mediated airway inflammation. Experiments: Overview: test causal pathway mTORC1 activation → altered metabolism (acetyl-CoA) → histone acetylation at Nmur1 locus → NMUR1 expression → NMU-driven ILC2 cytokine production → allergic inflammation. Animal models: C57BL/6 WT; Il5RFP-cre (R5/+) × Rptorf/f (ILC2-specific Raptor KO); Nmur1iCre-TdT and Nmur1iCre-TdT×Rptorf/f; Rag2−/−Il2rg−/− recipients; ROSA26iDTR crosses for ILC2 ablation. Human samples: PBMCs from n≥12 adult asthma patients and n≥12 matched healthy controls. Allergen challenges: papain, Alternaria alternata, and house dust mite (HDM) acute models defined by intranasal dosing schedules matched to the literature; NMU intranasal administration (20 μg/day × 5 days). Perturbations: rapamycin (4 mg/kg i.p. for 5 days), ACL inhibitor (ACLi, 30 μM in vitro; dose for in vivo per pilot PK), HAT inhibitor A-485 (1 μM in vitro; 50 mg/kg i.p. for in vivo as pilot), retroviral NMUR1 overexpression and GFP control. Primary endpoints: lung ILC2 frequency and absolute counts (flow cytometry gating lin-CD45+CD25+ST2+), intracellular IL-5 and IL-13 frequency and per-cell MFI, BALF eosinophil counts, lung histology mucin index (AB-PAS positive area), NMUR1 protein MFI, p-S6 and p-4E-BP1 MFI. Metabolic assays: Seahorse ECAR and OCR on sorted lung ILC2s; 2-NBDG glucose uptake; BODIPY lipid uptake; cellular citrate and cytosolic acetyl-CoA quantification. Epigenetic assays: ChIP-qPCR and ChIP-seq for H3K27ac and H3K9ac at Nmur1 locus; ATAC-seq for chromatin accessibility at Nmur1. In vitro functional assays: sorted ILC2 stimulation with IL-7 ± NMU ± IL-33; cytokines measured by ELISA and intracellular staining. Cell-intrinsic tests: adoptive transfer of WT or Raptor-KO ILC2s into Rag2−/−Il2rg−/− recipients followed by papain challenge; rescue experiments: retroviral NMUR1 expression in Raptor-KO ILC2s plus adoptive transfer. Baselines and controls: WT vehicle, WT+DMSO, KO+DMSO, KO+NMUR1 OE, rapamycin-treated WT and ILC2-depleted controls (DTR). Ablation study: HAT inhibitor treated vs vehicle and HATi-treated ILC2 adoptive transfer to naive recipients. Human validation: measure p-S6, NMUR1 expression, and IL-5/IL-13 production in ex vivo PBMC ILC2s ± rapamycin/HATi. Evaluation metrics: statistical comparisons of cell frequencies and cytokine levels (mean ± SEM), effect sizes, fold-change in NMUR1 expression and H3K27ac enrichment, ECAR/OCR parameters (basal glycolysis, glycolytic reserve, basal respiration, spare respiratory capacity), BALF eosinophil counts, histology mucin score. Sample sizes: power analysis to detect 30% change in primary endpoints with α=0.05 and power 0.8; anticipated n=6–10 mice per group for in vivo experiments, n≥4 biological replicates for in vitro metabolic and ChIP assays. Analyses: two-sided t-tests or ANOVA with multiple-comparison correction as appropriate; at least one ablation/ rescue comparison: Raptor-KO ILC2s ± NMUR1 overexpression; one pharmacologic ablation study: rapamycin-treated ILC2 adoptive transfer vs DMSO-treated ILC2s. Randomization and blinded outcome assessment for histology and flow analysis. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: incomplete or mosaic Cre-mediated Raptor deletion in ILC2s; insufficient sorted ILC2 numbers for metabolic (Seahorse) and ChIP-seq assays; off-target or systemic effects of rapamycin, ACLi, or HAT inhibitor confounding cell-intrinsic interpretation; retroviral overexpression artifacts or non-physiologic NMUR1 levels. Data and evaluation biases: variability in human PBMC samples (medication, disease heterogeneity), batch effects in sequencing and ChIP assays, gating subjectivity in flow cytometry. Scalability and compute: ChIP-seq/ATAC-seq on rare cell populations requires deep sequencing and increased cost; Seahorse throughput limited by cell yield. Limits to generalization: findings in mouse lung ILC2s may not translate to human disease or to ILC2s in non-pulmonary tissues; allergen models (papain/Alternaria/HDM) capture acute responses and may not reflect chronic asthma endotypes; systemic mTORC1 inhibition causes broad immunosuppression limiting therapeutic specificity. Potential confounders: compensatory metabolic pathways may mask acetyl-CoA effects; NMUR1-independent mTORC1 targets may account for residual phenotypes preventing full rescue by NMUR1 overexpression.
